title: Reprocess a run's rejected rows: etl rejects reprocess
description:
When rows are rejected for a cause that is fixed later (a currency the catalogue starts using before we add it, a customer in a country we have just started shipping to whose national phone number we cannot complete yet), the only way to load them today is to find the original export again and re-run it. The rejects already keep each row's fields, so this loads them from there.

- `etl rejects reprocess <run-id> [--json]` (`Pipeline.reprocess`) feeds the rejected rows of a succeeded `customers` or `products` run through the source's normaliser and loader as a new run of that source, with the path `rejects of run N`, under the source's run lock, in one load transaction like any run. It prints the new run.
- Only rejects whose payload is the row's field mapping are fed again; rows the reader could not split (a list of fields, a raw line) are left out. A payload `safe_payload` may have altered to store it (U+FFFD, or `inf`/`-inf`/`nan` text standing for a non-finite number) is rejected again with its own reason instead of being read as the source's row (`sink.kept_as_read`).
- Rows that fail again are rejected again under the new run. The reject ratio does not apply (every row of the input was rejected once); quality checks and the future-skew limit do. The skew limit counts from when the rows were read from the source, the start of the file run they came from, not from now: a time beyond it comes from a source clock that ran ahead, and once loaded it would outrank the changes made after it. Migration 0005 adds `etl.runs.source_read_at`, where a reprocess run records that time (NULL for file runs), so reprocessing a reprocess run keeps it. `IN_THE_FUTURE` is now a constant in `extract.py`.
- The rows are taken whatever the watermark and the watermark does not move: rejected rows are usually older than the window by the time their cause is fixed. Rows are read from `etl.rejects` a batch at a time on the load connection (keyset on line and id), so the run still holds three connections.
- Refused with exit 2: runs that did not succeed (their good rows were not loaded either, so the file should be run again), and `orders` runs: an order version loads whole, and the lines rejected along with another line of their version keep only `{order_id, position}`, so a version cannot be rebuilt from rejects.
- `Pipeline.run` and `reprocess` share `_run`/`_load`; a small `_Input` says where the rows come from and whether the read is incremental.

Tests: `tests/pipeline/test_reprocess.py` (rows loaded once their currency is known, rows dated ahead of their run staying rejected, also through a reprocess of a reprocess run, rows rejected again, malformed and altered payloads, refusals) and `tests/cli/test_rejects_commands.py`. README updated.

decoys.looks_like: A reprocess run builds its IncrementalWindow without the watermark (`IncrementalWindow(stored if incremental else None, ...)`), so every replayed row is admitted however old it is, and it never advances the watermark (`window.advance(newest) if incremental else None`, line 293). Rejected rows are typically days old, so this seems to let stale rows from an old export overwrite newer warehouse data that later runs loaded — a product's price or a customer's email rolled back to an old value — exactly what the incremental window exists to prevent.
decoys.why_correct: The window is only an optimisation that avoids re-reading rows; it is not what protects newer data. Every write goes through newer-wins: ProductsLoader.merge uses newer_wins_upsert (src/etl/load/upsert.py), whose ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE has `WHERE target.updated_at < excluded.updated_at`, so an older or equal incoming row leaves the stored one untouched; CustomersLoader.merge (src/etl/load/customers.py) closes or touches the current version only under `latest.updated_at > current.updated_at` and inserts a version only when the customer has no current one, so a not-newer row changes nothing. The base already relies on this for the lookback, which re-reads rows the warehouse holds (IncrementalWindow docstring). The `updated_at` it compares can be trusted as the file run's: a replayed row must not lie beyond the future-skew limit counted from when the source was read (`read_at=original.rows_read_at`: the start of the file run, carried from run to run in `etl.runs.source_read_at`), so a time from a clock that ran ahead never reaches the loaders, however many times the rejects are reprocessed. Not advancing the watermark only means later file runs may re-read a little more; advancing it to replayed rows could skip real rows. Orders, the one dataset where a partial version could replace a stored order, are refused.
decoys.valid_rebuttal: Old rows cannot overwrite newer ones: products go through newer_wins_upsert in src/etl/load/upsert.py, which only updates when the stored `updated_at` is strictly older than the incoming one, and CustomersLoader.merge in src/etl/load/customers.py only closes or touches a current version when the incoming row is newer (`latest.c.updated_at > current.c.updated_at`) and only inserts for customers without a current version, so a not-newer row is a no-op. The times compared are as trustworthy as a file run's: Pipeline.reprocess passes `read_at=original.rows_read_at` (RunRecord in src/etl/store/runs.py: `source_read_at`, recorded by runs.start for reprocess runs, else `started_at`), so `_load` applies the future-skew limit from when the file run read the source, also when a reprocess run is reprocessed. The window in IncrementalWindow is documented as a re-read saving, with newer-wins making re-read rows harmless. Leaving the watermark alone is the safe choice: it only controls which rows a file run skips. Orders, whose versions load whole, are refused by Pipeline.reprocess.
